name: Element.getHTML(), serializable shadow roots, and declarative shadow DOM. The cluster comprises: Element.getHTML(options) and its siblings ShadowRoot.getHTML() and Document.getHTML(); the options bag {serializableShadowRoots, shadowRoots}; the attachShadow({serializable: true}) flag and the ShadowRoot.serializable property that reflects it; declarative shadow DOM, written as <template shadowrootmode="open|closed"> with the companion attributes shadowrootserializable, shadowrootclonable and shadowrootdelegatesfocus; and the parsing counterparts Element.setHTMLUnsafe(), ShadowRoot.setHTMLUnsafe() and Document.parseHTMLUnsafe(). Historically this was proposed as getInnerHTML({includeShadowRoots}) before being renamed. Defined across the WHATWG DOM and HTML standards.
kind: Browser feature defined by a living standard (WHATWG HTML/DOM). Not a library, benchmark or service. It is the platform's own answer to the question this project has to answer -- how do you serialise a page whose content lives inside shadow roots -- and it answers it with an explicit, deliberate boundary at closed roots.
maturity: Production and interoperable. Baseline availability across current engines since September 2024, per MDN's own baseline marker; declarative shadow DOM itself shipped earlier (Chromium 90-era, WebKit and Gecko following, with WebKit publishing its support in 2023). The rename from getInnerHTML to getHTML happened during standardisation, so older articles and older code use the earlier name and the earlier option name includeShadowRoots -- worth knowing because searching on the old name surfaces a different and now-wrong API shape. The feature set is stable and in a living standard, so it can be extended but the current semantics are settled.
license: A royalty-free browser API in WHATWG living standards; no licence obstacle. The standard text is CC-BY-4.0. Nothing to vendor, nothing to license. Directly usable here.
keeps_and_discards: getHTML() serialises the DOM as it currently stands into an HTML string, which means it keeps the CURRENT node tree -- post-script, post-hydration, post-mutation -- rather than the originally delivered markup. That distinction is the whole reason it is more useful than re-fetching. Concretely it keeps elements, attributes as they currently are, text and comments, and -- only when asked -- the contents of shadow roots, emitted as declarative <template shadowrootmode=...> blocks that a parser can turn back into shadow roots. Without options it is byte-for-byte equivalent to innerHTML and shadow roots are simply absent, so any tool that reads innerHTML on a web-component page is silently dropping the content. What it discards is everything not expressible in markup, and the list is long and consequential: FORM-CONTROL PROPERTY STATE (input.value, checkedness, selectedness, indeterminate, the dirty-value flag) is not serialised because those are IDL properties, not content attributes, so a filled-in form serialises as an empty form; CANVAS PIXELS, video frames and WebGL state; CSSOM state that never touched a style attribute, including insertRule edits and adoptedStyleSheets, which is the standard way modern components carry their styles and which therefore vanishes; scroll positions, focus, selection, and top-layer state for open dialogs and popovers; event listeners; JavaScript state of custom elements; CSS generated content from ::before/::after, list markers and counters, which is user-visible text that is not in the DOM at all and therefore cannot be serialised by any DOM serialiser; and cross-origin iframe content, which is unreachable by policy. The honest summary is that getHTML captures the node tree faithfully and captures the PAGE partially, and the gap between those two is the same gap item 24 catalogues for the delta channel -- the two share a blind-spot list because they share a substrate.
structure_preserved: Complete for the node tree, including nesting, sibling order, attributes and comment nodes, and -- uniquely among DOM serialisers -- SHADOW BOUNDARIES, which is why this API matters here. Each serialised shadow root appears as a <template> carrying shadowrootmode, and optionally shadowrootserializable, shadowrootclonable and shadowrootdelegatesfocus, so the boundary, its mode, and its behavioural flags all survive the round trip explicitly rather than being flattened away. That is a materially better structural contract than a composed-tree flattening, which loses the boundary irreversibly. Two structural things are NOT preserved: SLOT ASSIGNMENT, since the serialisation records the light-DOM children and the shadow tree separately and leaves re-assignment to be recomputed on parse, which is correct but means the flattened tree is derived rather than recorded; and MANUAL slot assignment (slotAssignment: 'manual'), where the assignment is JavaScript state with no markup representation and is lost outright. For a project folding the COMPOSED tree, the second is a real hole -- a manually-slotted component serialises into markup that reparses into a different composed tree.
interactive_elements: Controls are serialised as elements with their content attributes, which means their DECLARED configuration survives and their STATE does not. A button's disabled attribute, an input's type and name and placeholder, an anchor's href, a form's action, aria-* attributes, role, tabindex and contenteditable all survive verbatim. This is exactly the tag-plus-interactivity substrate the project wants, delivered by the platform with no heuristics involved: the serialisation makes no judgement about what any element is for. The gap is state, below.
interactive_state_fidelity: Split cleanly along the attribute/property line, and knowing which side a given state falls on is the practical skill here. PRESERVED, because attribute-reflected: disabled, readonly, required, hidden, open on details and dialog, the popover attribute, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-checked, aria-disabled, aria-current, role, tabindex, contenteditable, and the CHECKED and SELECTED attributes as authored. NOT PRESERVED, because property-only: an input's current value (the value attribute holds the default, not the state), a checkbox's or radio's checkedness after any user or scripted interaction, an option's selectedness likewise, input.indeterminate, input.files, textarea's current value, and form validity state. The practical consequence is stark and should be stated in any capture built on this API: a serialised checkout form looks pristine no matter what the user typed into it. That is simultaneously a fidelity defect and a privacy feature -- see legal_basis_and_pii_posture. Token cost of the preserved state is essentially free, since the attributes are already in the serialisation; the accessibility tree beats markup on this axis only because it exposes the computed property state that markup structurally cannot, which is the real reason the AX tree is not simply redundant with a good HTML serialisation.
layout_awareness: None. getHTML performs no layout, reads no geometry, and does not force style resolution; it walks the node tree and writes markup. It is therefore trivially compatible with no_layout_in_the_fold, and it is one of the few page-reading operations that provably does not trigger a reflow, which also means it does not perturb the page's own performance profile in a way the page could time. Its consequence is the inherited one: a serialisation cannot tell a rendered element from a display:none one except by reading the STRING content of a style attribute or a class name, which is a string operation on DOM data and stays inside the fold.
javascript_required: The API is JavaScript, so yes trivially. More usefully: it does not require the PAGE's scripts to have run, but it reflects whether they have. Called at document_start you get the parse-time tree; called after load you get the hydrated tree. This makes it the correct instrument for capturing a client-rendered page without re-fetching, and it means the capture's meaning depends entirely on WHEN it was called -- a timing that must be recorded as capture metadata or the artifact is uninterpretable. Note the important asymmetry with fetch-based capture: getHTML sees content the server never sent, and misses nothing the server sent that scripts later removed. Calling it does not itself fire telemetry, since it makes no network requests and dispatches no events.
evaluation_method: Correctness is established by specification algorithms plus web-platform-tests, run by all three engines -- the strongest and most vendor-neutral evaluation regime available for a browser feature. What is NOT evaluated by anyone is FIDELITY in the sense this project needs: no test suite asks whether a getHTML serialisation, reparsed, reproduces a page a user would recognise, and no study measures what fraction of real pages' content lives in shadow roots at all. The right evaluation to run locally is the round-trip fixed point: serialise with getHTML({serializableShadowRoots: true}), reparse with parseHTMLUnsafe or setHTMLUnsafe, serialise again, and compare. It is oracle-free, it is cheap, and it directly measures the property the project cares about. A second, more demanding evaluation is capture-versus-live: serialise, reparse into a detached document, and diff the resulting composed tree against the live one -- which surfaces the slot-assignment and adoptedStyleSheets losses that a pure string round trip hides because they are absent from both sides.
corpus_size_and_origins: Not applicable to a browser feature; web-platform-tests uses synthetic documents. The relevant empirical unknown is population-level and unmeasured anywhere: what fraction of real pages use shadow DOM, what fraction of THOSE use closed mode, and what fraction mark their roots serializable. Anecdotally closed roots are used by a minority but a strategically important minority -- browser-internal UI, some widget and payment embeds, and libraries that deliberately encapsulate against third-party scripts -- and the serializable flag is opt-in and therefore rare, since almost no author has a reason to set it. Those two facts together determine how much of the modern web this API can actually capture, and nobody has published the numbers. Measuring them on the project's own 136-page, 109-origin corpus would be a genuinely novel and directly decision-relevant result, and it should be reported per archetype rather than as an aggregate.
reported_precision_recall: None exist and none are meaningful for a serialiser -- it is exact for what it covers. The figures that would matter and are unpublished: the fraction of pages where getHTML with serializableShadowRoots:true captures strictly more than innerHTML; the fraction where content remains unreachable because roots are closed and unserializable; and the round-trip fixed-point rate over a real corpus. The project's own measured position is the closest available datum: a projection drawing 80.9% of a page's affordances against a capture holding 99.7% suggests the capture side is close to complete for the affordances measured, which in turn suggests shadow-root loss is not the dominant term in that particular gap -- but that inference is not a measurement of this API and should not be presented as one. [uncertain] throughout.
independent_oracle: Yes, two, and both are cheap. (1) The serialise-reparse-serialise fixed point, which needs no reference at all and catches escaping errors, attribute-order instability and shadow-root emission bugs. (2) A comparison against an independently produced capture of the same page -- an outerHTML walk, a CDP DOM.getOuterHTML, or a full manual traversal of the composed tree -- which shares the DOM but not the serialisation code, and therefore catches serialiser-specific loss. Neither is a full oracle for user-visible fidelity, which would require rendering both and comparing, and that requires geometry and belongs in the actuator layer.
evidence_independence: Multi-vendor standard, cross-engine test suite, public results: as close to vendor-neutral as it gets, and there is nothing here to launder. MDN's baseline marker (available across latest browsers since September 2024) is compiled from browser-compat-data rather than asserted by a vendor. The only claims to treat carefully are the security ones -- the assertion that getHTML's attribute escaping of angle brackets prevents mutation-XSS is a design rationale drawn from security research rather than a measured guarantee, and it should be reported as a hardening measure, not as proof of safety.
page_archetype_coverage: Varies with component architecture rather than with content type, which is a different axis from the rest of this research set and worth stating. Pages built with plain server-rendered HTML -- most articles, documentation, forums, and government sites -- have no shadow roots at all, so getHTML with options is exactly equivalent to innerHTML and the feature buys nothing. Pages built on web components -- design-system-heavy enterprise applications, some e-commerce product pages, embedded widgets, media players, and increasingly server-rendered component frameworks that emit declarative shadow DOM -- can have the majority of their meaningful content inside shadow roots, where innerHTML captures a skeleton of empty custom-element tags and getHTML captures the content. So this feature's value is bimodal: irrelevant on most of the web, decisive on a growing minority, with no middle. Service and checkout flows are the worst archetype overall because they combine component-heavy UI with the form-control property state this API cannot serialise.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Script- and locale-invariant. Serialisation is a mechanical walk emitting text and attribute values with HTML escaping applied; it performs no tokenisation, segmentation, case folding or normalisation, so CJK, RTL and whitespace-free scripts survive byte-identically. The one interaction worth naming is that the serialiser emits whatever code points the DOM holds, so if the page's text is in NFD it stays NFD -- the round trip is normalisation-preserving, which is correct, and means any normalisation the project wants must be applied deliberately downstream and applied identically on both sides of any comparison.
leaks_outward: Nothing. getHTML is a synchronous, in-process read with no network activity and no observable side effect on the page. It fires no events, dispatches no mutation records, and does not cause resources to load -- note the contrast with an approach that reconstructs a page by re-fetching its subresources, which announces itself to every third-party host on the page. This is a meaningful privacy property: reading a page this way tells nobody anything.
mechanism_detectability: Very low, and this is the API's decisive advantage over the alternative for reaching shadow content. Calling getHTML is not observable from page script: it mutates nothing, so the page's own MutationObserver sees nothing; it dispatches nothing; and there is no reflection API that reveals a call happened. Contrast the alternatives directly, because this is the whole reason the item matters. PATCHING attachShadow to capture references to closed roots is detectable by any of several one-line checks -- Function.prototype.toString on Element.prototype.attachShadow returning a non-native body, comparing the function identity against a fresh same-origin iframe's realm, or checking property descriptors -- and the project refuses it on exactly that ground. Driving the page through CDP has its own known detection surface. getHTML has neither. The residual detectability is second-order and small: serialising a very large tree costs CPU and lengthens the task, which a page instrumenting frame timing could in principle notice, and the mitigation is to serialise incrementally per subtree rather than the document in one call. One further point deserves emphasis: the shadowRoots option ACCEPTS closed roots, but only if you already hold a ShadowRoot reference, and the only way to hold a reference to a closed root you did not create is to have intercepted its creation. So the API does not provide a bypass -- it provides a serialiser that will honour a reference you legitimately have, which for a page's own code is useful and for an external observer is not. The closed boundary holds, by design, and this API confirms rather than weakens it.
countermeasures: For the reader: serialise per subtree rather than whole-document to flatten the timing signature; never patch a platform function; never mutate to mark what has been read; enumerate open shadow roots by walking element.shadowRoot rather than by any interception. For the page defending itself: closed shadow roots remain a working defence against external serialisation, and NOT setting serializable is the default, so authors get encapsulation without effort. A page can also defeat serialisation-based capture by keeping content in canvas or in CSS generated content, both of which no DOM serialiser can reach. There is no countermeasure available to the reader for any of these, only declaration -- record that closed roots were present and how many, so the capture advertises its own incompleteness.
measured_fidelity_cost: Unmeasured in the literature and measurable here. The specific quantities: (a) content captured by getHTML({serializableShadowRoots:true, shadowRoots:[...open roots...]}) versus innerHTML alone, per page, as a fraction of text and elements -- this measures what the feature buys; (b) content still unreachable because roots are closed, which is the hard ceiling and the number that decides whether the closed-root constraint costs anything material; (c) the reparse discrepancy, i.e. composed tree after round trip versus live composed tree, which measures the slot-assignment and adoptedStyleSheets losses. Control for all three is the live composed tree as walked directly. None of these has a published value.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented; a serialisation is a string with no metadata. Because getHTML captures the page as currently rendered, a capture taken while a consent banner is displayed contains the banner, and a capture taken after dismissal does not -- so the gate state is present in the CONTENT and absent from the record, which is the worst arrangement because it silently contaminates a corpus while looking like content. Gate state must be recorded out of band at capture time. The one relevant advantage over fetch-based capture is that an in-page serialisation naturally reflects the operator's actual session state, including logged-in views, which is a fidelity gain and a privacy hazard in equal measure and should be flagged as both.
determinism: Deterministic for a fixed DOM and a fixed engine: the HTML fragment serialisation algorithm is fully specified, attribute order follows the element's attribute list order, and the output is a pure function of the tree. Two caveats. First, attribute ORDER reflects the order attributes were set, so two DOMs that are semantically identical but were built in different orders serialise differently -- a real problem for any byte-comparison of two captures, and the mitigation is to canonicalise (sort attributes) before comparing rather than to expect the serialiser to do it. Second, and more consequentially, the DOM itself is not deterministic on a live page: a serialisation taken at two different moments differs for every reason a page changes, so run-to-run reproducibility is a property of the page, not of the API. The serialiser is the reliable part of an unreliable pipeline.
determinism_across_versions: The serialisation algorithm is standardised and cross-engine, so the output format is stable in shape. What drifts is what is in the tree to serialise: HTML parser differences and changes (whitespace text nodes, implied tbody, template and slot handling, error recovery) mean the same source page yields different DOMs and therefore different serialisations across engines and across versions of one engine. There is also a documented cross-engine variation in the SECURITY escaping: some browsers serialise angle brackets in attribute VALUES as entities to block mutation-XSS round-trip attacks and others historically did not, so byte-identical output across engines is not guaranteed even for an identical tree. Practical consequence: never diff serialisations produced by different engines or different browser builds without normalising first, and record the browser build in capture metadata. Baseline support beginning September 2024 also means older browsers lack the API entirely, so a capture pipeline must either pin a modern browser or carry a fallback that will silently drop shadow content.
reproducibility: High if the inputs are frozen, low against the live web -- the same conclusion as every other item here, but with an unusually clean remedy available. Because getHTML with declarative-shadow-DOM output and parseHTMLUnsafe/setHTMLUnsafe form a matched serialise/parse pair, a captured string is a genuinely re-loadable artifact: the capture can be reparsed later, in a fresh context, into a DOM with its shadow boundaries intact, and every downstream computation re-run against it deterministically. That is a stronger reproducibility story than a flattened text capture, which cannot be reparsed into a structured page at all. The recommendation follows directly: store the getHTML string as the frozen capture artifact and treat it, not the live page, as the input to any measured pipeline. The unfixable residue is the discarded state list -- form values, canvas, adoptedStyleSheets, manual slot assignment -- which no reparse restores.
failure_modes: (1) SILENT SHADOW LOSS: calling getHTML() with no options, or innerHTML, on a component-heavy page returns a skeleton of empty custom-element tags with all content missing, and looks like a successful capture. This is the single most likely failure and it is invisible. (2) CLOSED ROOTS: content in closed roots is unreachable without a reference; the capture is incomplete with no error. (3) UNSERIALIZABLE OPEN ROOTS: an open root not marked serializable is skipped by serializableShadowRoots:true, and must be passed explicitly in the shadowRoots array -- so the correct call requires first WALKING the tree to collect every element.shadowRoot, which is an O(page) traversal the API does not do for you, and forgetting it produces a partial capture that also looks successful. (4) MANUAL SLOT ASSIGNMENT loses its assignment on round trip, producing a reparsed page whose composed tree differs from the original with no error. (5) ADOPTED STYLESHEETS AND CSSOM edits are absent, so a reparsed capture is unstyled or differently styled -- irrelevant to a layout-blind fold, relevant to anything that later renders the capture. (6) FORM STATE loss, as above. (7) CANVAS, VIDEO and CSS GENERATED CONTENT unreachable by any DOM serialiser. (8) SIZE: whole-document serialisation of a large application produces a very large string in one allocation, which on a big page is a memory spike and a long synchronous task. (9) setHTMLUnsafe/parseHTMLUnsafe are named 'unsafe' for a reason -- they parse scripts and declarative shadow DOM without sanitisation, so reparsing a captured hostile page in a live context executes it; captures must be reparsed only in an inert document or with scripting disabled.
failure_visibility: Silent for every fidelity failure, loud for none. There is no warning when shadow content is skipped, no signal when a closed root is encountered, no indication that adoptedStyleSheets were dropped. The API returns a plausible string in every case. This is precisely the pattern the project refuses elsewhere and the remedy is the same as in item 24: compute a declared-incompleteness flag set during the capture walk -- number of open shadow roots serialised, number of closed roots encountered and skipped, presence of canvas, presence of cross-origin iframes, presence of manual slot assignment, presence of adoptedStyleSheets, count of form controls whose property state was not captured -- and attach it to the artifact. All of these are cheap to detect during the traversal that collecting shadow roots requires anyway, so the incompleteness report costs almost nothing on top of the capture.
scale_limits: Cost is linear in serialised node count with a large constant for string building, and the practical limit is memory rather than time: a whole-document getHTML on a large application produces a multi-megabyte string synchronously. The shadow-root collection walk that correct use requires is a separate O(page) traversal. Neither is superlinear, but both are O(page), which is the relevant point: getHTML is a FULL-CAPTURE instrument, not an incremental one, and every call pays for the whole subtree. Per-subtree calls make the cost proportional to the subtree, which is how it should be used in a delta-driven design -- serialise only the subtree a mutation record named.
delta_cost_model: getHTML has no delta model of its own; it is an O(subtree) operation by construction, and that is the correct way to think about its role. Composed with a mutation-record stream it fits a delta design well: when a childList record names an added subtree, getHTML on that subtree costs the subtree and nothing more, which is exactly the bound the record itself implies. What falls OUTSIDE the per-change cost: (1) the INITIAL capture, which is O(page) and unavoidable; (2) the SHADOW-ROOT DISCOVERY WALK, which must be repeated because attachShadow generates no mutation record -- newly added elements can be checked as they arrive, but a shadow root attached to a pre-existing element is invisible until a periodic O(page) rescan finds it, so shadow correctness costs an amortised full scan; (3) DECLARATIVE SHADOW DOM in the initial parse, which is present before any observer exists and is therefore only ever obtained by the initial full capture -- an argument for using getHTML rather than a mutation replay as the base state; (4) SLOT REASSIGNMENT, which changes the composed tree without changing the node tree and therefore without changing any subtree's serialisation in a way a record would point you at; (5) attribute changes, where re-serialising a whole subtree to capture one attribute edit is enormous over-payment, so the delta path must apply attribute records directly and reserve getHTML for structural additions; (6) the PERIODIC FULL RECAPTURE that soundness requires, O(page) by construction; (7) everything the serialiser cannot see at all -- form property state, canvas, CSSOM -- which has no cost because it is never captured, and whose absence is the exception that must be declared rather than a cost that must be bounded.
reanchoring_stability: Not an anchoring mechanism, but it interacts with anchoring in one important way: because getHTML preserves shadow boundaries explicitly as template elements with a mode attribute, a serialisation-derived address can distinguish 'inside shadow root of host X' from 'light-DOM child of host X' unambiguously, which a flattened composed-tree address cannot. That makes shadow depth a recoverable component of the key rather than something that must be carried out of band. Conversely, positional addressing over the serialised form has the usual fragility, and re-parsing a capture can produce a subtly different tree from the live one (whitespace handling, implied elements, manual slot assignment loss), so addresses derived from a reparsed capture are not guaranteed to match addresses derived from the live DOM -- a real hazard if the project computes addresses at capture time and re-computes them at analysis time from the stored string. Compute once, store the address, and validate the round trip.
adversarial_exposure: A serialiser preserves everything in the node tree regardless of visibility, so hidden, off-screen, zero-size and aria-hidden content all survive into the artifact on equal terms with visible content -- the standard layout-blind exposure, neither better nor worse than any DOM read. Three specifics. (1) Getting shadow content is a net INCREASE in exposure relative to innerHTML: injections planted inside a shadow root were previously invisible to naive extractors and become visible here, which is correct for fidelity and expands the attack surface for anything that feeds the capture to a model. (2) The parse side is genuinely dangerous: setHTMLUnsafe and parseHTMLUnsafe are the only way to reconstitute declarative shadow DOM and they are explicitly unsanitised, so reparsing a captured hostile page in a live, scripting-enabled context is remote code execution against the analysis environment. Any reparse must happen in an inert document. (3) The one point where this API is actively PROTECTIVE: getHTML escapes angle brackets inside attribute values as entities specifically to prevent mutation-XSS round-trip attacks, in which a string that is safe when parsed once becomes an executable construct when serialised and reparsed. That is a real, deliberate hardening of the serialise-parse round trip and it is directly relevant to any pipeline that stores markup and later reloads it. Regarding the layout-blind ceiling: as with the rest of this design, the concealment classes reachable without geometry are the Unicode-level ones, the attribute-declared ones (hidden, aria-hidden, tabindex=-1) and the inline-style-declared ones readable as strings out of the style attribute -- all of which survive into a getHTML capture and are therefore inspectable. Stylesheet-driven concealment does not survive, since the stylesheet's effect is not in the markup, so a getHTML capture cannot even in principle support the analysis that would catch it.
provenance_carrying: Partial and improvable. The serialisation itself carries no origin, no timestamp and no address -- it is a bare string. What it DOES carry that most alternatives do not is shadow structure, so shadow depth is recoverable from the artifact rather than needing separate bookkeeping, and the mode attribute records whether each boundary was open or closed. Everything else -- URL, capture time, browser build, gate state, whether scripts had run, which roots were skipped -- must be attached as a wrapper around the string, and the failure to do so is the most common way such artifacts become uninterpretable. The recommendation is that the stored capture is never the raw string but a record of (url, capture time, browser build, script-state marker, gate state, incompleteness flag set, serialisation string), and that per-node provenance is derived by addressing into the reparsed tree rather than being embedded in the markup, which would corrupt the round trip.
roundtrip_safety: This is the API's strongest property and the reason it belongs in this research set. getHTML({serializableShadowRoots: true}) and setHTMLUnsafe/parseHTMLUnsafe are a MATCHED PAIR: the former emits shadow roots as <template shadowrootmode=...> and the latter is the parser mode that turns those templates back into shadow roots. So serialise -> parse -> serialise is designed to be a fixed point including shadow structure, which no other DOM serialisation mechanism offers. It is not an unconditional fixed point and the exceptions are worth listing because they are exactly the fidelity limits: manual slot assignment does not survive; adoptedStyleSheets do not survive; form-control property state does not survive; and attribute ORDER is preserved but not canonicalised, so byte-equality across independently constructed DOMs is not expected. The escaping policy is unusually strong for a browser serialiser -- text is HTML-escaped as normal, and attribute values additionally have angle brackets entity-encoded to defeat mutation-XSS on reparse. Recommendation: run the fixed-point test as a standing check on every capture, report the byte-difference rate, and treat a non-fixed-point capture as a loud failure rather than a curiosity. It is the cheapest oracle-free fidelity metric available anywhere in this research set.
token_budget_and_ordering: Raw serialised HTML is a poor thing to give a model -- it is the most token-expensive representation of a page there is, with attribute noise, framework-generated class strings and structural markup dominating the content -- so getHTML is a CAPTURE format, not a presentation format, and should never be emitted to a model directly. Its role in the token contract is upstream: it is the lossless, reparseable substrate from which a budgeted markdown projection is computed, and the fact that it is reparseable means the projection can be recomputed at a different budget later without re-visiting the page. The ordering implication is that the serialisation preserves document order exactly, so any ordering policy the projection adopts is a deliberate choice made downstream rather than an artifact of the capture.
representation_cost: Very high per page as a stored artifact -- full markup including every attribute, and on component-heavy pages the shadow-root templates add the component internals on top of the light DOM, so a getHTML-with-shadows capture is strictly larger than innerHTML and can be substantially so. Against that: it is the only capture from which the shadow-bearing structure can be reconstituted, and it compresses extremely well because markup is highly repetitive. What is lost per byte saved by NOT using the shadow options is the entire content of component-based pages, which is the wrong trade on any page that has it. In tokens: not applicable, since it should not be tokenised.
what_could_be_adopted: Five things. (1) getHTML WITH BOTH OPTIONS AS THE CANONICAL CAPTURE PRIMITIVE, preceded by an explicit walk collecting every reachable element.shadowRoot into the shadowRoots array -- because serializableShadowRoots:true alone silently misses every open root the author did not opt in, and almost no author opts in. This is the correct, non-detectable, standards-blessed way to capture shadow content and it should replace any use of innerHTML or outerHTML in the sensor. (2) THE SERIALISE-PARSE-SERIALISE FIXED POINT as a standing oracle-free fidelity test, with parseHTMLUnsafe in an INERT document, reported as a byte-difference rate per capture. (3) THE DECLARATIVE SHADOW DOM ENCODING as the storage format for shadow structure, so shadow depth lives in the artifact rather than in side metadata and a stored capture is genuinely reloadable. (4) THE ATTRIBUTE-ESCAPING POLICY -- entity-encoding angle brackets in attribute values -- as the template for the project's own escaping policy anywhere markup or markdown is stored and later reparsed, since it targets exactly the round-trip mutation class that a naive escaper misses. (5) THE INCOMPLETENESS FLAG SET computed during the shadow-collection walk, which converts this API's uniformly silent failure into a declared caveat. Explicitly NOT to be adopted: patching attachShadow to obtain closed-root references, which the shadowRoots option might superficially seem to enable and which the project correctly refuses as detectable; and any use of setHTMLUnsafe on captured content in a scripting-enabled context.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. The serialiser applies no content policy, names no region, and emits the tree as it is; it is the definition of a structure-agnostic read. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and notably it does not even trigger layout, so it neither reads geometry nor perturbs it. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AT SUBTREE GRANULARITY, WITH NAMED EXCEPTIONS. Per-subtree serialisation composes correctly with mutation records and costs the subtree; outside that bound sit the initial O(page) capture, the periodic shadow-root discovery rescan required because attachShadow emits no record, declarative shadow DOM present before any observer, slot reassignment which changes the composed tree without changing any subtree's serialisation, and attribute-only changes for which re-serialising a subtree is gross over-payment. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS and actively supportive -- the API exists only in a real browser against a real document, and the fixed-point test it enables is a real check rather than a stub. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AND CONSTRAINT-CONFIRMING, and this is the item's clearest verdict. The shadowRoots option will serialise a closed root, but only from a reference you already hold, and the only way to hold a reference to a closed root you did not create is to intercept attachShadow -- which the project refuses and which is independently detectable via Function.prototype.toString and cross-realm identity comparison. So the platform's own answer is exactly the project's: closed means closed, and the correct response is to DECLARE the resulting incompleteness rather than to defeat it. Using this API is affirmative evidence that the constraint is being honoured. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is, and it is the single best-fitting mechanism in this research set -- it is the platform's sanctioned, undetectable, round-trippable way to capture shadow-bearing pages, and its limits (closed roots, form property state, CSSOM, canvas, CSS generated content, manual slot assignment) are precisely the exception list that any honest fidelity or O(delta) claim has to publish.
governance_signal_handling: None, and none applicable: this is an in-page read of a document already loaded, not a retrieval. robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF, Web Bot Auth and HTTP 402 all govern fetching and are settled before getHTML is ever called; governance state belongs on the URL record the capture hangs from. One second-order point worth noting: because getHTML captures the RENDERED page including content the page's own scripts fetched from other origins, a capture can incorporate third-party content whose own governance signals were never consulted -- the serialiser has no way to know which parts of the tree came from which origin, and the composed markup erases that distinction. If per-origin governance matters, the network log must be captured alongside and correlated, because the serialisation alone cannot support it.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: A getHTML capture is a persistent copy of third-party page content and is therefore squarely the regulated act; it is materially MORE sensitive than a fetched copy of the same URL in one specific way and materially LESS in another, and both should be recorded. MORE: it captures the page as the operator actually saw it, so a logged-in view includes personalised content, account identifiers, private messages and any other authenticated material, none of which an anonymous fetch would obtain. That makes gate state a mandatory field and makes behind-login captures a distinct, higher-sensitivity retention class. LESS: because form-control property state is not serialisable, anything the operator TYPED into the page -- search terms, credentials, personal details -- is absent from the capture by default, and obtaining it would require a deliberate, separate mechanism. That default is the right one and should be preserved as a decision rather than left as an accident, since it means the most sensitive category of in-page data is excluded by construction. Erasure is well served: the capture is a single string keyed by URL, so prefix-scoped deletion removes it cleanly. [uncertain] on the specific lawful-basis analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject; the assessment here is structural.
